question: Who decides what an economy produces, how production is organised, who receives the output, and what rules govern those decisions—and how do those rules affect firms, investment, jobs and wages?

systems.name: Market-oriented
systems.ownership: Private ownership is prominent; households and firms make many decentralised choices.
strengths: Competition can reward innovation and efficiency
Entry allows new firms and ideas
risks: Market power and barriers to entry

systems.name: Command / centrally planned
systems.ownership: Public authorities direct major output, input, investment and price decisions; state ownership may be extensive.
strengths: Can mobilise resources toward selected priorities
Can coordinate large projects by central direction
risks: Weak incentives when targets and accountability are poor

systems.name: Mixed
systems.ownership: Private and public actors both make important decisions; government also taxes, regulates, provides and redistributes.
strengths: Can combine enterprise and price signals with public goods
Can address some market failures and protect people
Can support stability and wider access
risks: Poor design can add compliance costs
Outcomes depend on accountability and enforcement

keyCorrection: Market does not mean no government. Government involvement does not automatically mean command economy. Property, contracts, corporate law, liability, competition rules, taxation and dispute resolution define the rules within which markets operate.

institutions.definition: Durable formal or informal rules, norms, procedures and enforcement arrangements that structure repeated interaction.
functions: Clarify who owns, uses, transfers or earns returns from an asset.
Contracts and dispute resolution make exchange possible beyond personal trust.
Predictable rules reduce searching, negotiating, monitoring and enforcement costs.
Shared standards and procedures help firms, workers, lenders and customers plan.
Fraud rules, audits, liability and sanctions deter cheating and unsafe conduct.
Fair access and competition policy can limit exclusionary conduct.
Policy can respond to externalities, public goods, information gaps and market power.
Taxes, transfers, education, healthcare and social insurance shape opportunity and risk.
Monetary and fiscal frameworks affect inflation, credit, demand and employment.

distinction.institution: The rules of the game: e.g. company law, contract enforcement, limited liability and insolvency procedures.
distinction.organisation: The players: e.g. a company, court, ministry, trade union, bank, regulator or university.
distinction.example: A company is an organisation. The law governing its incorporation and contracts is part of the institutional framework. A regulator is an organisation; the statute defining its powers and accountability is an institution.

failures.name: Public goods
failures.definition: Generally non-rival and non-excludable: one person's use does not substantially reduce another's, and excluding non-payers is difficult.
failures.example: National defence and some forms of public knowledge.
failures.why: People may free-ride, so private markets can provide less than the socially desired amount.

failures.name: Externalities
failures.definition: A cost or benefit imposed on third parties that is not fully reflected in the transaction price.
failures.example: Pollution is a negative externality; knowledge spillovers and vaccination can create positive externalities.
failures.why: Private decisions may not include the full social cost or benefit.

failures.name: Other market failures
failures.definition: Information asymmetry, natural monopoly and market power can also distort outcomes.
failures.example: A dominant network provider may face weak competitive pressure.
failures.why: The market outcome may not be efficient under the relevant welfare criteria.

policy.caveat: Intervention can improve outcomes, but it has costs and can fail. Education, healthcare and transport are not necessarily pure public goods; access can be restricted and capacity can be congested.

governmentFailure: Regulatory capture by powerful regulated interests
Corruption, patronage, exclusion or selective enforcement
Contradictory procedures that raise entry costs
Policy uncertainty that discourages long-term investment

governance.intro: World Bank WDR 2017 identifies three functions that help policies work in real political and social settings.
items: Rules and promises remain credible over time.
People and organisations can align expectations and investment.
Actors contribute to shared goals rather than free-ride or block them.
governance.warning: Formal institutional design alone is not enough. Power asymmetries can cause exclusion, capture and clientelism; function, enforcement, power relations and local context matter.

causal.title: Institutions → exchange and investment
steps: More willingness to exchange and invest
causal.qualifier: A possible pathway, not an automatic guarantee.

causal.title: Institutions → firms and jobs
steps: Stable rules and fair market access
causal.qualifier: Infrastructure, skills, finance, technology, demand and management also matter.

causal.title: Market failure → policy response
steps: Private incentives diverge from social outcomes
causal.qualifier: The policy result depends on design, capacity, incentives and accountability.

india.label: India: a mixed economy with a changing policy framework

timeline.title: Planning and a significant public-sector role
timeline.detail: The state played a substantial role in strategic and basic industries; private enterprise continued within extensive licensing and controls.

timeline.title: Structural reforms
timeline.detail: Following macroeconomic imbalances and a balance-of-payments crisis, India liberalised trade and investment, simplified firm entry in many areas, reduced industrial licensing and expanded private-sector participation.

timeline.title: Gradual and uneven evolution
timeline.detail: Private participation expanded in areas such as telecom alongside a strengthened regulatory framework; public enterprises and state capacity remained important.

timeline.title: Welfare and social justice principles
timeline.detail: Directive Principles include reducing inequalities, securing adequate livelihood, distributing material resources for the common good and preventing harmful concentration of wealth. Article 37 says these principles guide governance but are not directly enforceable by courts.

india.employment: Policy in telecom, infrastructure, education, labour, tax, trade, procurement and finance can change which firms enter, where they invest, what skills they demand and how work is organised. No single reform explains India's IT industry.

countryLens: Market-oriented, with extensive regulation, taxation, public programmes and public spending.
Private firms and open markets combined with larger tax-funded welfare states and coordinated labour institutions.
Market exchange and private enterprise coexist with extensive state ownership and direction in strategic sectors and significant party-state influence.
jobs: Contract enforcement can support outsourcing, supplier relationships and startups.
Competition and entry rules affect the number of employers and workers' outside options.
Education and training institutions shape skill supply.
Labour laws, collective bargaining, minimum wages and social insurance affect conditions and bargaining.
Tax, procurement and infrastructure spending shift demand across industries and regions.
Corruption, exclusion and capture can protect incumbents and restrict opportunity.
salary: Institutions influence the labour-market environment; they do not mechanically set an individual's salary. Pay also depends on role, skills, productivity, scarcity, employer economics, labour supply, bargaining power, geography, selection and compensation structure.
limitations: Market and command are ideal types; real economies are hybrids and vary by sector.
A law on paper does not prove effective enforcement or equal access.
Institutions and development influence each other, so causal identification is difficult.
Cross-country comparisons face measurement, endogeneity and context problems.
Regulation can correct market failures and protect workers; poorly designed regulation can raise costs or protect incumbents.
Deregulation can improve entry in some settings but worsen externalities, market power or worker insecurity in others.
Government capacity and political incentives matter alongside formal design.
There is no single institutional blueprint that can be transplanted unchanged.
